1201.quote_or_event: “I drink in the sublime essence of the Lord. With the taste of this essence, I have forgotten all other tastes.”
1201.explanation: Bhagat Kabir says the sweetness of the Lord's Name is so great that every other drink and pleasure fades beside it.
1201.tie_back: The Kural says love is sweeter than toddy, because its joy does not run out even when it is only remembered; Kabir likewise rates the taste of divine love above every intoxicant.
1201.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 337, Raag Gauree, Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1201._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa), two consecutive lines; reasonable-to-strong fit on love's sweetness beating any drink, though Kabir does not stress joy from memory alone, the love is spiritual, and Sikhism rejects intoxicants outright.

1202.quote_or_event: “Remembering Him in meditation, happiness comes, and all sorrows and pains simply vanish.”
1202.explanation: Guru Arjan teaches that simran, remembering the Lord, brings joy and makes all pain disappear.
1202.tie_back: The Kural says love is sweet in every way because thinking of the beloved brings no pain at all; Gurbani likewise says that remembering the Beloved drives every sorrow away.
1202.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 518, Raag Goojaree, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1202._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa); strong fit on remembrance of the beloved as free of pain, though simran is meditation on God's Name rather than a lover's memories.

1203.quote_or_event: “Good omens and bad omens affect those who do not keep the Lord in the mind.”
1203.explanation: Guru Arjan rejects reading omens: only those who have forgotten the Lord are troubled by signs of good or bad luck.
1203.tie_back: The Kural's wife reads a sneeze that fades as a sign her husband has stopped thinking of her; Gurbani would tell her that omens have no hold on one whose mind is fixed on the Beloved.
1203.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 401, Raag Aasaa, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1203._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa); next-best match offered as an honest contrast: Sikhism rejects omen-reading of the kind the Kural's folk belief about sneezing assumes, though both link signs to whether the beloved is remembered.

1204.quote_or_event: “Kabeer, my mind has become immaculate, like the waters of the Ganges. The Lord follows after me, calling, "Kabeer! Kabeer!"”
1204.explanation: Kabir says that once his mind was made pure, the Lord Himself came after him, calling his name.
1204.tie_back: The Kural's wife knows her beloved lives always in her heart but anxiously asks whether she has a place in his; Kabir gives the answer of mutual love: the Beloved remembers the devoted one and calls after him.
1204.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1367, Saloks of Bhagat Kabir (salok 55) (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1204._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa), both lines of salok 55; reasonable fit on whether the beloved also remembers the one who loves, but Kabir is confident where the Kural is anxious, and the condition is a pure mind, not a lover's devotion.

1205.quote_or_event: “I do not forget the Lord in my mind.”
1205.explanation: Guru Arjan speaks of a mind in which the Lord is always present and never forgotten.
1205.tie_back: The Kural's wife teases that her beloved, who has barred her from his own heart, keeps coming into hers without a pause; Gurbani likewise describes a Beloved who never leaves the devotee's mind.
1205.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1120, Raag Kaydaaraa, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1205._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa); next-best match: it shares the beloved's constant presence in the mind, but lacks the Kural's playful accusation that he barred her from his heart, which has no Gurbani counterpart.

1206.quote_or_event: “She weeps, thinking of her Husband Lord, and she cherishes His virtues; her Husband Lord does not die, and does not leave.”
1206.explanation: In the Alaahanee (songs of mourning) in Raag Vadhans, Guru Amar Das describes the soul-bride who keeps her Husband Lord alive in her heart by remembering His virtues.
1206.tie_back: The Kural's wife says she stays alive only by remembering the days she spent with him; the soul-bride in Gurbani likewise lives by remembering her Beloved's virtues, with tears.
1206.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 583, Raag Vadhans, Alaahanee, Guru Amar Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1206._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa); reasonable fit on sustaining love through tearful remembrance, though the bride remembers the Lord's virtues rather than shared days, and Gurbani adds that this Husband never truly leaves.

1207.quote_or_event: “When You come to mind, I am totally in bliss. One who forgets You might just as well be dead.”
1207.explanation: Guru Arjan says that remembering the Lord brings complete bliss, while forgetting Him is a kind of death.
1207.tie_back: The Kural's wife never forgets her beloved, and though remembering burns her, she asks what would become of her if she forgot; Gurbani gives the same answer, that to forget the Beloved is to die.
1207.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 749, Raag Soohee, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1207._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa); strong fit on forgetting the beloved as death, though for Guru Arjan remembering brings bliss rather than the Kural's scorching pain, and the love is spiritual.

1208.quote_or_event: “He does not know any bitter words; the Perfect Lord God does not even consider my faults and demerits.”
1208.explanation: Guru Arjan describes the Beloved Lord as never harsh, never speaking a bitter word, and never holding the devotee's faults against them.
1208.tie_back: The Kural's wife takes comfort that however much she thinks of her beloved he is never angry with her for it; Gurbani likewise praises a Beloved who never answers with anger or bitter words.
1208.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 784, Raag Soohee, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1208._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa); reasonable fit on a beloved who never grows angry, but the Kural's wry humour (he cannot object to what he cannot see) is absent, and the kindness is God's grace.

1209.quote_or_event: “You are me, and I am You-what is the difference between us?”
1209.explanation: Bhagat Ravidas declares that the devotee and the Lord are not really separate, going on to compare them to gold and the bracelet made of it, or water and its waves.
1209.tie_back: The Kural's wife recalls her husband's old vow, 'We two are not separate,' and her life ebbs as she sets it against his present unkindness; Ravidas makes the same vow of oneness, but as a truth the separation cannot break.
1209.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 93, Sri Raag, Bhagat Ravidas (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1209._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa), punctuation as given there; reasonable-to-strong fit on the words 'we are not separate', though in the Kural they are a broken lover's vow and in Ravidas a spiritual oneness of soul and God.

1210.quote_or_event: “If You are the moon, then I am the partridge in love with it.”
1210.explanation: Bhagat Ravidas compares his devotion to the chakor, the partridge of Indian poetry that gazes at the moon all night.
1210.tie_back: The Kural's wife begs the moon not to set, so that her eyes may find the beloved who went away but never left her heart; Ravidas uses the same moonlit image of eyes fixed in longing on the Beloved.
1210.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 658, Raag Sorath, Bhagat Ravidas (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1210._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa); reasonable but partial fit: both use the moon as the focus of a lover's longing gaze, but in Ravidas the Lord is the moon, while in the Kural the moon is a go-between through which she hopes to see her husband.
